steps.body: Division word problems mix both kinds freely, so the reading matters more than the arithmetic.
steps.narration: Division word problems mix both kinds freely, so the reading matters more than the arithmetic.

widget.prompt: 6 litres poured into 1/3-litre cups — slide to the number of cups.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low — each cup takes only a third of a litre, so six litres fill many of them.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — six litres cannot fill more than eighteen third-litre cups.
widget.successFeedback: 18 — three cups per litre, across six litres.

predict.prompt: 6 litres into 1/3-litre cups — more or fewer than 6 cups?
predict.reveal: Each litre fills three cups, so the count is well above the number of litres.

cml.actionGoal: Ask what is being cut and how big each piece is, then count the pieces for g5fd story.
invariants: Division and fractions are the same act seen twice: sharing a wholes among b people gives a/b, and dividing BY a piece asks how many of it fit, which is why g5fd story produces a larger answer when the divisor is under one.
misconceptions: Reading "divide by 1/4" as "take a quarter of", reporting a remainder when the leftover could be shared, or shrinking the pieces when only their count should change.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the divisor grew past one, would the answer become larger or smaller than the dividend?

widget.prompt: Compute 9 × 4 — the number of fourths that fit in 9 wholes.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding mixes a count of wholes with a piece size; each whole holds 4 fourths.
4 is how many fourths fit in ONE whole; there are 9 wholes here.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Ask what is being cut and what size the pieces are; the count of pieces is the answer.

widget.prompt: Compute 9 ÷ 3 — sharing 9 equal pieces among 3 people.

commonErrors.feedback: 9 is the WHOLE pile; the question asks what one of 3 equal shares holds.
Subtracting removes one share once; sharing equally is division.

widget.prompt: A 6-litre container fills 1/3-litre bottles. Which computation finds the number of bottles?

options.label: 6 ÷ 1/3 = 18, because you count how many thirds fit
options.feedback: Correct — the question asks how many bottles, so count the thirds that fit in 6 litres.

options.label: 6 × 1/3 = 2, because the bottles hold thirds
options.feedback: That finds one third of 6; it does not count the number of one-third-litre bottles.
That divides one bottle's capacity among 6, reversing the quantities in the story.
Subtracting removes the capacity of one bottle only; filling every bottle requires division.
